# C++ Object Pool Debugging

## Problem

## Overview

This is the second part of a C++ software-engineering online assessment (the first part is three algorithm problems
in C++). You get 45 minutes and a mostly written **object pool**: a class template that hands out pre-constructed
`ObjectT` slots, obtains memory in fixed-size **batches**, and keeps every unused node on an intrusive singly linked
**free list**. The code you are handed does not compile -- it has several deliberately simple mistakes -- and
`numAllocated()` is left for you to write. Make it build, make it behave as documented, and implement
`numAllocated()` so that every test case passes.

```cpp
template <typename ObjectT>
class ObjectPool {
public:
    struct Node { ObjectT object; Node* next; };

    Node& getNode();                 // hand out one node; allocates a new batch when none is free
    void releaseNode(Node& node);    // give a node back
    size_t capacity() const;         // nodes owned by the pool (handed out + free)
    size_t numAllocated() const;     // nodes handed out and not yet released -- implement this

private:
    struct Batches { Batches* next; Node* nodes; size_t size; };
    Node* allocateBatch(size_t batchSize);
};
```

## What is in the workspace

- `src/ObjectPool.h` -- the pool, the only file you edit.
- `src/main.cpp` -- the test driver (locked in the assessment). It reads a scripted session from stdin
  (`get <handle> <orderId> <price> <qty>`, `release <handle>`, `show <handle>`, `capacity`, `allocated`), runs it
  against an `ObjectPool<Order>`, and after destroying the pool prints `live <n>`, the number of `Order` objects
  still alive.
- `tests/input/` + `tests/output/` -- 12 sessions with their expected output: 2 samples and 10 standing in for the
  hidden cases (empty pool, an exactly full batch followed by growth, batch size 1, out-of-order releases, drain and
  refill, long random sessions).
- `tickets/T1-does-not-compile.md`, `tickets/T2-num-allocated.md` -- the two things the prompt asks for.
- `run.cmd` / `run.sh` -- compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra` and judge every case
  (`PASS` / `WRONG ANSWER` / `RUNTIME ERROR` / `TIMEOUT`).

## Parts

1. **Make it compile.** Fix the mistakes in `ObjectPool.h` without redesigning it; the interface used by the driver
   stays the same. Read the warnings as well as the errors.
2. **Make it correct and implement `numAllocated()`.** Once it builds, the test sessions show whether the pool hands
   out valid nodes, reports its capacity, and cleans up everything it allocated. `numAllocated()` must return the
   number of nodes currently handed out.

Rules: keep the batch + free-list design; callers release each node at most once; single-threaded.

## How it is evaluated

`run.cmd` exits 0 only when the header compiles and all 12 test cases produce exactly the expected output, including
`live 0` at the end of every session. In the assessment the judge is the same stdin/stdout comparison; an
interviewer reviewing the code also looks at whether you stated the pool's invariant (every node is either on the
free list or handed out) and fixed the code in place instead of rewriting it.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Fix the compilation errors first without redesigning anything - scan for missing semicolons after struct definitions, inconsistent identifier spelling, and malformed template declarations.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

State the pool's invariant before writing the new method: capacity is the sum of all batch sizes, and the free list chains exactly the nodes not currently handed out.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

Derive the answer from that invariant rather than adding new bookkeeping, walking the free list to count what remains available.

</details>
